profile.a: The author, writing individually for Behavioural Finance.
Managers of a retail mutual fund in the course's simulated scenario, choosing between polluting (P) and clean (C) US stocks.
Whether pollution is priced as a risk factor (compensation for exposure) or a behavioural factor (mispricing from investor preferences).
Handed in on 28 February 2025, after the SEC's 2022 proposal on climate disclosure.
US listed firms, within the UN SDG agenda and UK, US and EU regulation.
Regulation and ESG fund flows are moving capital away from polluters; the fund must know whether the higher return on P stocks is a reward for risk or a mispricing to exploit or avoid.
Reviews regulation, sustainability rankings, mutual fund risk tools and factor models (Fama-French three- and five-factor) and concludes in favour of the risk explanation.

facts.what: UN goals cited as the policy pressure on polluters
Ranking used to screen sustainable firms

facts.value: Fama-French three-factor (1993), with five-factor (2015) as extension

facts.what: Scenario figures analysed in the text

charts.title: Polluting and clean firms as the paper describes them

left.title: Polluting firms (P)
items: Exposed to carbon pricing and stricter rules
Litigation, carbon tax and reputational risk
Screened out by ESG funds, facing divestment

right.title: Clean firms (C)
items: A 'green premium' that can lead to overvaluation
Lower future returns as a result

charts.takeaway: The fund faces a trade-off between ethical alignment and return: P pays more, C carries less risk but may be over-priced.

charts.title: The causal chain behind the 'risk factor' verdict

items.title: Policy tightens
items.text: SDG-driven rules, SEC disclosure and carbon pricing target high emitters.

items.title: Costs rise
items.text: Polluters pay for cleaner technology, compliance and reporting.

items.title: Profits become uncertain
items.text: Transition and climate risk weigh on profitability and valuation.

items.title: Investors demand more
items.text: Higher expected returns compensate for holding that exposure.

items.title: Pollution behaves as a priced risk
items.text: So the fund should model it with factor tools, not treat it as a bias to exploit.

charts.title: Weight of argument in the paper (points made for each explanation)
text: 6 points: regulation, carbon cost, transition risk, disclosure, divestment, litigation
2 points: ESG sentiment, overvaluation of clean firms
charts.takeaway: The verdict follows a one-sided case. The behavioural side gets two points, and the strongest evidence for it (investor preference lowering green returns) is in the reading list but not used.
charts.source: Count of the distinct arguments made on pages 56-59.

charts.title: What the fund is told to do

items.title: Model the risk
items.text: Use a factor model so returns are judged net of market, size and value.

items.title: Tilt, don't exclude
items.text: Lean towards low-carbon firms while keeping enough diversification.

items.title: Integrate ESG
items.text: Build pollution risk assessment into stock selection.

items.title: Watch for overvaluation
items.text: Use contrarian checks so clean stocks are not bought at a green premium.
